chapter_theme: The ninth ten calls things poor (நல்கூர்ந்தன்று): goods and acts that lose their worth because the condition that would give them force is missing, such as a land without a just king, desire and adornment in the very old, sulking where one is not cherished, words where words do not carry, anger that inspires no awe, and visits where there is no friendship.

81.reading: The land of a king who rules without justice is said to be impoverished.
81.nuance: Line 1 is the frame shared by every ten. Here நல்கூர்தல் is literal as well as figurative: an unjust reign makes the country itself poor, not only the king's name.

items.claim: the country of a king without justice is poor

82.reading: The desire of a woman who is very old is reckoned a poor, wretched thing.
82.nuance: மிகமூத்தோள் is feminine: the saying names a woman, where the next old-age line (86) uses the masculine முதிர்வுடையோன். The judgement is of fitness to age, a norm of the period about women's bodies, and the line gives no reason beyond the frame.

norm.note: a period judgement that an old woman's desire is unbecoming

items.claim: the sexual desire of a very old woman is poor

83.reading: Joining with one who is close to you yet bears you enmity is reckoned a poor thing to do.
83.nuance: Our text has உறவோனை, one related to you; tamilvu has உறைவோனை, one who lives with you. Either way the person is near and hostile, so the sense holds: alliance with an enemy within gains nothing.

items.claim: joining with a hostile intimate is poor

84.reading: The pleasure that comes to a man lying sick is reckoned poor.
84.nuance: கிடந்தோன், the one laid down by disease: the pleasure is real but cannot be enjoyed, so it counts for little.

items.claim: pleasure got by one bedridden with illness is poor

85.reading: Sulking where one is not cherished is reckoned poor.
85.nuance: Read as தன் போற்றாவழி, where the other does not cherish one; the printed spacing (தன்போற் றாவழி) splits போற்றா. Sulking is a lover's play that works only when the other cares enough to appease it.

items.claim: sulking where one is not cherished is poor

86.reading: Ornament on the body of one who is very old is reckoned poor.
86.nuance: முதிர்வுடையோன் is masculine, so this old-age line, unlike 82, is about a man; adornment cannot restore what age has taken.

items.claim: adornment on an aged man's body is poor

87.reading: Speaking where one's word does not carry is reckoned poor.
87.nuance: Our text reads சொற்சொல்லாவழி, 'where a word is not spoken', which gives little sense beside சொலவு; tamilvu's சொல் செல்லாவழி, 'where a word does not go', is read here. On our text the line might instead say that talk is poor where nothing worth saying is said.

items.claim: speech where words have no effect is poor

88.reading: Drawing near to one who is empty within is reckoned poor.
88.nuance: அகம் வறியோன் may be one empty of heart (without love or understanding) or one whose house is bare; the first fits a ten on worthless acts better, but the second, approaching a poor man to ask, cannot be excluded.

items.claim: approaching one hollow within is poor

89.reading: Anger where it inspires no awe is reckoned poor.
89.nuance: உட்கு is the dread a person commands; anger in one who has none is empty show, measured by its effect rather than judged as a vice.

items.claim: anger where there is no awe behind it is poor

90.reading: Going to a place where there is no friendship is reckoned poor.
90.nuance: சேறல், going or visiting: the visitor where no friendship waits gets nothing and loses standing, so the ten closes on a social act as it opened on a political one.

items.claim: going where there is no friendship is poor

links.note: Kural 559 says that when the king bends justice the sky bends and withholds rain; the line says the land of a king without justice is poor.
links.teaches: The couplet gives a mechanism, the failed rain, and the line gives only the result, a poor land, so together they show the period's chain from royal injustice through the weather to the country's want.
links.list_adds: It sets the unjust king's land first in a ten of things that fail for lack of their ground, so misrule becomes the type of all such emptiness rather than a cosmic exception.

links.note: Line 26 says those living under a king who keeps no justice do not openly censure him; line 81 says his land is poor.
links.teaches: Read together, the subjects keep silent about an unjust king but the land itself shows the injustice through its poverty, so the blame the people withhold is spoken by the country.

links.note: Naladiyar 13 says aged men who cling to desire in the house have no path to safety; the line calls a very old woman's desire poor.
links.teaches: The quatrain condemns aged desire because it bars release, and the line condemns it with no thought of release and names a woman, so the pair shows one judgement on old age held on ascetic grounds and on plain worldly fitness.
links.list_adds: It places the old woman's desire among ten misfits of condition (a sick man's pleasure, an old man's ornament), judging it as unfitting rather than as a danger to the soul.

links.note: Both lines set an aged body against a good of youth: desire in an old woman (82), ornament on an old man (86).
links.teaches: The ten applies the same verdict to both sexes, desire for the woman and adornment for the man, so the pairing shows how the period divided what each was faulted for in age.

links.note: Kural 890 likens living with those not in accord to sharing a hut with a snake; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
links.teaches: The couplet stresses the danger of living beside the hostile, the line the futility of allying with them, so together they show the enemy within is both a threat and a bad bargain.
links.list_adds: It moves the couplet's fear into a reckoning of worth, counting such a union among things that are simply poor, which the snake image does not do.

links.note: Thirikadugam 4, item 3, counts taking into one's hand a man who once raged against one among the acts of one bound for death; the line calls joining with a hostile intimate poor.
links.teaches: Thirikadugam calls the embrace of a former foe deadly and Muthumozhikkanchi calls it worthless, so the same act is judged by its danger in one list and by its yield in the other.

links.note: Line 5 ranks freedom from bodily disease above youth; line 84 calls the pleasure of a sick man poor.
links.teaches: The first ten ranks health above youth and the ninth shows why, since disease empties even pleasure, so health appears as the ground other goods stand on.

links.note: Kural 1308 asks what use suffering is where no lover knows of it; the line calls sulking poor where one is not cherished. Both turn on an absent beloved's care (இல்லா வழி, போற்றாவழி).
links.teaches: The couplet speaks of grief with no one to notice and the line of sulking with no one to appease it, so together they show that every display of hurt in love has worth only before someone who cares.
links.list_adds: It takes a lover's sulk out of the Kural's love book and sets it among public ills like misrule and empty anger, treating it as one more act that fails without its ground.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 27, item 3, calls beauty in those without means painful; the line calls ornament on an aged body poor.
links.teaches: One list makes beauty depend on wealth and the other makes adornment depend on youth, so together they show that beauty in these works is never good alone and fails when either support is gone.

links.note: Kural 720 likens speaking before those not of one's set to nectar spilled in a drain; the line calls speech poor where words do not carry.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the waste in the hearers' unfitness, the line in the word's lack of force, so together they show that speech fails either from the audience or from the speaker's standing.
links.list_adds: It puts futile speech beside futile anger (89) and futile sulking (85) in one ten, making each a case of an act without the power to land.

links.note: Kural 301 says restraint of anger counts only where anger can take effect; the line calls anger poor where it inspires no awe.
links.teaches: The couplet says restraining powerless anger is no virtue, and the line says indulging it is no gain, so together they show that anger without power is worth nothing whether held back or let loose.
links.list_adds: It judges anger by its effect, as one of ten things emptied by a missing condition, where the couplet judges the restraint of anger as a virtue.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 21, item 2, calls going to eat with those who do not share their food painful; the line calls going where there is no friendship poor.
links.teaches: Innaa Narpathu names the particular case, the stingy table, and the line states the general rule behind it, so together they show the visit's worth lying in the host's bond, not in what is offered.

source_issues: 81: the comparison site's text lacks line 2, the saying itself; our text has it after the frame line.
81, 89, 90: parenthesised letters (அரச(ன்), உட்(கு), நட்(பு)) are editorial restorations in our text.
83: our text has உறவோனை; tamilvu has உறைவோனை ('one who dwells with you'). The sense is close either way.
87: our text has சொற்சொல்லாவழி; tamilvu has சொல் செல்லாவழி, which gives the better sense and is read here.
83-90: the printed spacing splits words across sandhi (நல் கூர்ந்தன்று, போற் றாவழி, முதிர்வுடை யோன்).
